tool.intro: In a difficult moment, we often talk to ourselves harshly. This short break, inspired by the work of Kristin Neff, invites you to treat yourself as you would treat a friend going through the same thing.
tool.prepare: Think of a situation that is weighing on you right now — not the hardest one, a moderate one to start with. Allow yourself to feel a little of the discomfort it brings.

steps.title: Acknowledge this moment
steps.text: Notice what you are feeling, without judging or minimising it.
steps.phrase: 'This is a moment of difficulty.' or 'This hurts right now.'

steps.title: Remember you are not alone
steps.text: Difficulty is part of everyone's life. Other people, right now, are feeling something similar.
steps.phrase: 'I'm not the only one going through this.' or 'Everyone goes through moments like this.'

steps.title: Offer yourself kindness
steps.text: If it helps, place a hand on your heart or somewhere soothing. Feel the warmth of your hand. Then ask yourself what you need.
steps.phrase: 'May I be kind to myself.' or 'May I give myself the patience I need.'

tool.ownWords: If these phrases don't speak to you, find your own words: what would you say to a dear friend in the same situation?
tool.done: Take a moment to notice how you feel now. It's normal for this to feel uncomfortable at first: self-kindness is learned, like any skill.
tool.credit: Exercise inspired by Kristin Neff's 'self-compassion break'.

howItWorks.title: How Self-Compassion Works
howItWorks.description1: Self-compassion means treating yourself with the same kindness you would offer a loved one in difficulty. It is not self-pity or making excuses: it is recognising your suffering and responding with care.
howItWorks.description2: The break rests on three elements described by psychologist Kristin Neff: mindfulness (recognising what you feel), common humanity (remembering suffering is part of everyone's life) and self-kindness.
howItWorks.description3: Self-criticism often adds a layer of suffering to anxiety. Learning to speak to yourself gently can help you get through difficult moments with a little more calm.

mindfulness.title: Acknowledge
mindfulness.description: See what you feel, without judging or exaggerating it.

humanity.title: Share
humanity.description: Remember that others go through similar difficulties.

kindness.title: Take care
kindness.description: Speak to yourself as you would speak to a friend.

science.title: What Studies Say
science.description: Programmes that train self-compassion have been evaluated in many trials. The short break offered here is one of their basic exercises.
science.bottomLine: learning to be kind to yourself can reduce anxiety, stress and self-criticism. It is a skill that grows with practice.

meta.title: What many trials show
meta.who: Very diverse participants: students, stressed adults, people with health problems.
meta.what: Self-compassion training programmes, compared with groups with no programme or another activity.
meta.result: The programmes reduced anxiety, low mood, stress and self-criticism (medium effects), and rumination markedly.
meta.caution: Programmes varied widely between trials, often in groups; effects were clearer in groups than individually.

whenToPractice.title: When to Practice
items: When you are blaming or harshly criticising yourself
After a mistake, a setback or an awkward situation
When anxiety comes with shame or discouragement
Every day, so this kind outlook becomes more natural

whatYoullNotice.title: What You Might Notice
items: A slight sense of relief, or an emotion rising: both are normal
An inner voice that is a little less harsh
Feeling less alone with the difficulty
With practice, an easier time supporting yourself in hard moments

start.title: Start small
start.description: First choose a moderate difficulty, not the most painful situation.

emotion.title: If emotion rises
emotion.description: Gentleness sometimes stirs up emotions. Slow down, breathe, and return to a grounding exercise if needed.

words.title: Your own words
words.description: The suggested phrases are just a starting point: keep the ones that speak to you.
